aidb_assessment.novelty: High: the work evaluates compaction prospectively through controlled downstream execution rather than retrospective summary similarity.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The controlled design and extensive appendices make this a strong evaluation template. Adoption should await public artifacts, replication across executors and prompts, within-task boundary comparisons, and more completely documented human validation.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: High for agent-memory evaluation. It distinguishes actionable state preservation from factual coverage and identifies epistemic status, completed work, pending obligations, and located resources as evaluation targets.

executive_summary: CompAct-Bench evaluates context compaction by its effect on subsequent agent completion rather than summary similarity. It controls compacted length, executor, restored environment, and remaining action budget across Search, Coding, and Workspace tasks. Under aggressive compaction, even the strongest model retains limited downstream reliability. Stage effects reverse by domain: later Search worsens while Coding improves, consistent with repository state preserving materialized progress. Key threats are selection of reliably solved tasks, one boundary per trajectory, executor dependence, an internal Workspace suite, imperfect length calibration, and incompletely documented human validation.

assumptions: Consistent success in screening makes the reference execution stable enough to attribute later degradation mainly to compaction.
Deterministic action replay reconstructs a sufficiently comparable environment although outputs need not be byte-identical.
Character-length matching provides a useful cross-provider control despite not matching tokenizer usage or full assembled-context length.
Holding one compacted context fixed across fresh continuations separates rollout variability from compaction-generation variability.
Findings obtained with the selected prompts, executors, tools, and evaluators meaningfully represent compaction capability.
key_components: A process-level benchmark built from successful agent trajectories without reference summaries.
Separation of the evaluated compactor from fixed downstream executors and task evaluators.
Character-level Iterative Ratio Calibration for approximately matched compacted-output lengths.
Reconstructed boundary environments and continuation budgets matched to the reference remainder.
Bootstrap uncertainty, execution-stage comparisons, without-history controls, state-persistence analyses, and trajectory-grounded error annotation.
method.overview: The authors screen tasks with three executor runs, retain only consistently solved tasks with nontrivial histories, and select one successful reference trajectory. Each trajectory is assigned to an early, middle, or late compaction boundary. The pre-boundary interaction body is compacted once while the system/task head remains verbatim. Iterative Ratio Calibration controls character length. Three fresh continuations resume from the boundary environment with fixed executors, tools, evaluators, and a matched remaining-action budget; strict success is averaged across continuations.

open_questions: Will model rankings and failure modes replicate with different executor families?
Does iterative calibration alter content quality relative to one-shot length-matched compaction?
Can explicit fields for confirmed facts, rejected hypotheses, completed work, pending obligations, constraints, and located resources reduce distortion?
Do within-task evaluations at every boundary reproduce the reported stage effects?
What accuracy–cost frontier appears when recovery budgets exceed the reference remainder?
Can full human annotation validate the reported error prevalence and behavioral associations?

problem.importance: Finite context windows make context management necessary, but a concise retrospective summary can still omit or distort facts, progress, epistemic status, constraints, and unresolved obligations needed for future actions.
problem.scope: The study covers information seeking, software engineering, and workspace automation. It evaluates robustness of previously successful executions after an intermediate handoff, not general task-solving ability or a complete production memory policy.
problem.statement: The paper asks whether a shorter model-generated representation of accumulated interaction history preserves enough working state for an agent to finish a long-running task.

proposed_experiments.baseline: The shared free-form compaction prompt with the same compactor, calibration target, executor, environment state, and action budget.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: A structured handoff separating confirmed facts, hypotheses, rejected alternatives, completed work, pending work, constraints, and located resources improves downstream completion at the same length budget.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired difference in strict Avg@3 accuracy; secondary blinded-human rates of premature commitment, lost resolution, and progress/state loss.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Complete both conditions for every retained public task; reject the hypothesis if the paired confidence interval does not exclude no improvement or length matching fails.

proposed_experiments.hypothesis: The Search decline and Coding improvement across stages persist under within-task boundary evaluation.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired within-task change in strict Avg@3 accuracy across early, middle, and late boundaries, reported separately by domain.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Complete every eligible public task at every boundary; reject the hypothesis if trend direction reverses or the paired interval includes no stage change.

proposed_experiments.baseline: The original boundary environment and compacted context without a progress ledger.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: A machine-readable progress ledger persisted in the environment reduces dependence on free-form compacted context, especially for Search and pre-edit Coding states.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Strict Avg@3 accuracy, with repeated-work actions and budget-exhaustion rate as secondary metrics.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Complete the preregistered paired public-task sample; reject the hypothesis if accuracy does not improve and neither secondary metric decreases.

results.result: Stage effects reverse by domain: Search falls from 52.9% at the 25% boundary to 42.6% at 50% and 34.6% at 75%, whereas Coding rises from 64.0% to 72.7% and 86.1%. Nine of twelve compactors decline monotonically on Search, while ten rise monotonically on Coding.

results.context: The controlled comparison supports the state-persistence account: repository progress can survive independently of text, while compacted context adds value at later boundaries. Its observed early-boundary increment is negative.

results.result: Among failed continuations, an annotated compaction error occurs in 92.5% of early failures and 85.8% of budget exhaustions. Critical omission is associated with +18.2 points of repeated work, progress/state loss with +13.8, and constraint/goal distortion with +10.5 points of unverified commitment.
